prompt.context: Your client is an American party-plan selling company that sells power tools through hosted parties (similar to Tupperware). The company has a small core of full-time corporate marketing staff that recruits consultants (independent contractors). The consultants recruit hosts, who hold the parties. Hosts invite purchasers to buy power tools; hosts are compensated with free gifts and discounts. Consultants earn a percentage of their hosts' sales, and can recruit up to four layers of other consultants, earning a portion of those consultants' revenues as well. The company started eight years ago and had explosive revenue growth. Recently the rate of growth has started to slow.
prompt.question: The client has asked you two questions: (1) What is the factor slowing growth? (2) How can they improve the situation?

clarifying_info.q: Has purchaser behavior changed — average frequency or size of purchase?
clarifying_info.a: No. Purchaser behavior has not changed; on average they buy as much and as frequently as before.

clarifying_info.q: Have hosts changed their behavior — number of parties or attendees?
Are consultants recruiting as many hosts as before?
Are consultants recruiting as many other consultants as before?
clarifying_info.a: No — the number of consultants being recruited has dropped, both via corporate marketing and via existing consultants.
No — the same incentive arrangement was in place during the period of explosive growth.

exhibits.title: Revenue Over Time
exhibits.shows: A line/bar chart showing the company's annual revenues over approximately 14 years (years 1–14 on the x-axis, revenue in units 0–700 on the y-axis), illustrating explosive early growth that has recently begun to slow.
exhibits.data: Y-axis: 0 to 700 (revenue units); X-axis: years 1 through 14; growth curve rises steeply then flattens in later years

framework: Map the four levels of the selling chain: (1) Purchasers, (2) Hosts, (3) Consultants, (4) Central marketing/corporate
Isolate which level is causing the slowdown by checking whether behavior or recruitment has changed at each level
Identify root cause at the level where recruitment has dropped (consultants recruiting other consultants)
Assess whether the cause is structural/incentive-driven or a saturation/market exhaustion issue
Develop recommendations: domestic geographic expansion into under-covered areas and/or international expansion

questions.prompt: Walk through the four levels of the selling chain. At which level is the problem occurring, and why?
questions.guidance: The candidate should systematically check each level top-down or bottom-up. Purchasers: no change. Hosts: no change. Consultant-to-host recruitment: no change. Consultant-to-consultant recruitment: this is where the drop occurs. The root cause is market saturation — the existing pool of consultants has essentially exhausted their social networks; nearly everyone interested in participating in power-tool party recruiting has already done so in the served areas.

questions.prompt: What might explain the drop in consultant recruitment even though the incentive structure has not changed?
questions.guidance: A strong candidate recognizes that incentives are a red herring — the compensation arrangement was the same during the explosive growth phase. The real issue is that the addressable pool of willing recruits in existing geographies has been depleted. The candidate should resist the temptation to focus on incentive mathematics (e.g., dilution across four layers) and instead focus on what has changed: market saturation.

math.setup: Illustrative incentive dilution: if each consultant earns 10% of the sales of consultants they recruit, then $1 of Consultant D's sales yields $0.10 for C, $0.01 for B, and $0.001 for A.
math.answer: By layer 4 the financial incentive for top-layer consultants to recruit is negligible — but this structure existed during explosive growth too, so it is not the new factor causing the slowdown.

brainstorming.prompt: Now that we know growth has saturated domestically, what options does the client have to restore growth, and specifically what would you look for in international expansion?

categories.name: Domestic geographic expansion
ideas: Map existing consultant coverage to identify under-served US regions
Direct corporate marketing spend into coverage gaps (e.g., states like New Mexico with low penetration)
Offer extra incentives to consultants who recruit in targeted under-covered areas

categories.name: International market selection criteria
ideas: Presence of a strong and growing DIY (do-it-yourself) culture
Legality and cultural acceptance of party-plan / direct selling (e.g., party-plan selling is illegal in China but common and accepted in Latin America)
Language and cultural proximity to reduce entry friction (e.g., UK shares common language with US)
Market size and growth rate of the DIY or home-improvement segment
Regulatory environment for independent contractor / multi-level sales structures

categories.name: Product and model adaptation
ideas: Assess whether power tools resonate with the target country's homeowner/DIY demographics
Consider localized product assortment or pricing
Evaluate whether the party-plan format is socially accepted in target culture

categories.name: Operational considerations
ideas: Identify local partners or master consultants to seed the network
Understand import duties, product safety certifications, and distribution logistics
Plan for currency and payment method differences

recommendation: The primary driver of slowing growth is domestic market saturation — existing consultants have exhausted their recruiting networks in covered geographies, not a change in incentives or purchasing behavior.

To restore growth, the client should pursue a two-track strategy: (1) domestic geographic expansion into under-covered US regions using targeted corporate marketing and consultant incentives, and (2) international expansion into markets with strong DIY culture and legal/cultural acceptance of party-plan selling — Latin America is particularly attractive, and the UK offers lower entry friction due to shared language.
risks: Party-plan companies can be fad-driven; the business model may face another saturation cycle in new geographies after initial growth
International expansion introduces regulatory risk (party-plan selling is illegal in some markets such as China) and operational complexity
Incentive dilution across four consultant layers may reduce motivation at the top level to invest in new geographic markets
next_steps: Conduct a geographic coverage analysis to map consultant density versus population across all US regions
Screen international markets against DIY-culture, legal, and cultural-acceptance criteria to prioritize 2–3 target countries
Pilot expansion in one domestic under-served region and one international market (e.g., a Latin American country) before committing to broad rollout
